items.gist: The guru traverses the tattva and bhuvana paths to reach the kalā path, where the varṇa form of consciousness rests for the yogin.
Varṇas are created with unrestricted powers and, resting in consciousness, bear true consciousness in non-difference.
Even untaught perceivers attain varied cognition through natural saṃskāras, while convention depends on this natural varṇa-consciousness.
Without rest, convention would be endless; speech and conceptual thought are rooted in convention, yet the infinite varṇa family expands through consciousness-reflection.
Māyīya varṇas arise independently of convention, and even a dull person can become a knower by following their sequence.
Through gaining autonomy, one masters the varṇa aggregate and experiences increasing wonder as the natural form is distinguished.
Absorption in the first māyīya varṇas yields poetic and eloquent capacity, culminating in rest in consciousness.
Resting in consciousness, one knows and does all; speech and omniscience are only meaningful if grounded in that consciousness.
The sixfold self appears through mātṛ-māna-meya relations, and purification of the path is attained through the body.
The guru purifies by inclusion or subtle refinement, leading to seed-state, mastery, renunciation, Śiva-nature, absorption, and release.
Mantras are variegated purifiers; anuttara trika mantras are always universal, while others have contextual primacy.
Purification extends to impurity, triads of goddesses, deities, faces, and limbs; all purification is Śiva's autonomy in non-difference.
All appears in the Lord as reflection, not externally; in Śiva-consciousness, embodied distinctions are like rope-snake illusion.
Pre-death doctrines are dream-like; appearances arise by general manifestation, and māyā-level forms are like variegated stones.
Worlds arise according to Śiva's will, not independently; Bhairava stands in consciousness-space when convention is unrooted.
In non-difference with Bhairava, the sense of 'I am this' is the differentiator; no other agent is established, as in dream.
One who knows plays in the city of consciousness, and birth-death variety appears self-created on consciousness's screen.
In truth consciousness alone is place and time; if creation were material, no support could be found within it.
At the end of the support-supported series, consciousness-Śakti, Śiva's form, supports all; the universe rests in its own support.
From dense 'I am this' to 'I am consciousness,' Bhairava-nature is completed; in Śiva, appearances have no real origin or decay.
Creation in space and time is incoherent; Śiva creates space and time, and dreamers independently measure directions and times.
No instant is truly fixed; those who reduce beings to an instant rely on empty views.
Śiva freely empties existents and clarifies non-existents; the Lord is the all-form, not any separate earth.
This has been stated before and need not be re-examined; thus the detailed exposition of the kalā path is concluded.
